title: Why coffee makes some people buzz and others barely notice
description: Sleep researchers often recommend avoiding caffeine for at least six hours before bedtime.Dr Lindsay Browning, a psychologist and sleep expert, says t
body: Sleep researchers often recommend avoiding caffeine for at least six hours before bedtime.Dr Lindsay Browning, a psychologist and sleep expert, says the evidence suggests caffeine might not just stop you dozing off but can affect the quality of sleep as well."I'll suggest to people that they might want to avoid caffeine after about 2pm if they are going to bed around 10pm," she says."But a blanket hard-and-fast rule isn't helpful, because it doesn't really allow for the intricacies and the individualisation of what's really going on."The NHS advises pregnant women, external to keep caffeine intake below 200mg a day, about two mugs of filter coffee, as studies have linked it to low birth weight and other complications.For other adults the key message is moderation, as sensitivity to caffeine varies so much from person to person."Caffeine is relatively safe," says Peter Rogers, emeritus professor of nutrition at the University of Bristol."If you consume a great deal of it, you just start feeling jittery and unpleasant and you start realising, 'I need to stop this, there's no point taking any more'." Caffeine overdoses are very rare and severe poisonings almost always involve concentrated caffeine products, where several grams can be swallowed in a matter of minutes.For coffee lovers the good news is that, if anything, that regular (if expensive) morning habit is linked to better health outcomes. While researchers cannot prove that coffee is the only reason, decades of studies suggest that people who drink it in moderation tend to have lower risks of several major diseases and may even live slightly longer than non-drinkers.

schema.headline: Why coffee makes some people buzz and others barely notice

title: Palace in war of words with Earl Spencer over book's claim on Charles and Diana
description: Buckingham Palace is in a war of words with Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, over a controversial memoir about her life and deat
body: Buckingham Palace is in a war of words with Earl Spencer, the brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, over a controversial memoir about her life and death.King Charles is accused of insensitively saying to Earl Spencer, in the wake of Diana's death in 1997, that "we'll forget her soon enough", according to excerpts published in the Daily Mail.But the Palace has pushed back unusually strongly, angered by the claims and attempting to cast doubt on them."While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.The language is reminiscent of Queen Elizabeth's unexpectedly firm response to claims of racism by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in 2021, with the comment that "recollections may vary".And the row threatens to overshadow a very crowded day for the royals - with the King, Prince William and Catherine attending events and Prince Harry making his first big appearance since returning to the UK.Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, to be published next week, seems set to reopen a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family - written from the perspective of her own Spencer family.The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's sudden death. And this book will give an insider's view on those events.In the published excerpt, Earl Spencer claims the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession.Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."It's a claim that's being rejected by the Palace, who see it as being entirely out of character for a man with a deeply compassionate nature, who at the time was dealing with his own grief and that of their two sons.Julian Payne, the monarch's former communications secretary, told the BBC that the King's apparent comments in the book were "just not language that I recognise".He said the "highly unusual" statement from the Palace demonstrated the "strength of feeling that there must have been for them to feel that they needed to go out there and correct it".The dispute comes when multiple royal events will be jostling for attention.King Charles is set to intervene in the debate about artificial intelligence, calling on AI industry leaders to prevent it becoming a destructive force."Those in our world who value our humanity and its vital moral component are anxiously seeking your reassurance that we will not lose control of our destiny," the King is expected to say on Thursday, as he hosts a gathering of leading AI firms at an Dumfries House, in Ayrshire."The development of AI, its substance and its pace, are both intriguing and deeply concerning in equal measure," the King will say.The rapidly-advancing technology has raised fears about its safety, as well as a threat to jobs.The King will be joined by AI minister Kanishka Narayan and representatives of tech firms such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia and Google DeepMind. He will ask the question about how the benefits of AI can be harnessed while still ensuring that it remains safe, and raise the issue of whether there can be international co-operation in protecting it from being misused."The decisions taken at this formative time will shape the world inherited by future generations," he will say. "And so, the task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world."Meanwhile, during the day, Prince William and Catherine will visit community and volunteering projects on the Isle of Bute.The couple - who are called the Duke and Duchess of Rothesay in Scotland, rather than the Prince and Princess of Wales - will make their first official visit to the town of Rothesay.They will see the traditional sport of shinty, visit a community-owned pub and hear about those working to protect the island's natural environment.

schema.headline: Palace in war of words with Earl Spencer over book's claim on Charles and Diana

title: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter
description: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMo
body: Figure caption, Low expectations that Russia's election will bring peace closer, Steve Rosenberg reportsBySteve RosenbergRussia editorReporting fromMoscow and DmitrovThe system of power in Russia is often referred to as "managed democracy" (where the Kremlin does the managing).That means huge powers for the president and few political surprises.This weekend's election is set to deliver another parliament dominated by the party of power, United Russia, and a house of MPs fiercely loyal to Vladimir Putin.Critics dismiss the vote as neither free nor fair.But the Kremlin doesn't care what the critics say."We have our own political system, our own political process," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov explained recently.That means no curveballs for the Kremlin. No surprises. So no story?Far from it.For the Kremlin, the election of 450 deputies to the lower house of parliament, the Duma, is important. This is the first parliamentary election here since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The Kremlin will use it to claim that most Russians back the president and the war, as well as to promote the political careers of soldiers back from Ukraine: officials say nearly two hundred war veterans are taking part in the election.Image caption, This election is being used to promote the political careers of some military veteransAs for the election campaign, that has provided a window on Russian society four-and-a-half years into the war.I said no surprises. But there have been some."Good evening and welcome to tonight's campaign speeches by candidates for Duma Electoral District 158," said the anchor on state TV.The studio director cut to a wide shot revealing six empty lecterns."The candidates haven't turned up," admitted the host. "So, it's goodbye from me."In another TV debate (where the politicians were present) one crooning candidate sang his pitch:"The Communist Party, onwards we go!"We're with the people, don't you know?"More X Factor than exit poll.Yet a musical manifesto is strangely appropriate. In the previous Duma, everyone seemed to be singing from the same hymn sheet. At the final session of parliament in July, MPs stood and applauded as the speaker of the house chanted repeatedly:"Russia, Putin, Victory! Russia, Putin, Victory!"It was a signal that all MPs in parliament should back President Putin and the war.Image caption, Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov [centre] backs the war in Ukraine"All parties in the Duma, every single one, voted in favour of 170 laws to support the special military operation," Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov told me with obvious pride about the last parliament."In that sense there is 100% agreement in the Duma."I caught up with Zyuganov on the campaign trail outside Moscow at a bread and biscuit factory. As I watched rows of identical-looking loaves speeding along the conveyer I thought about Russia's parliament. It's not that all parties in the Duma are identical: some are more nationalist, others – like Zyuganov's party - more left-wing. But when it comes to backing the Kremlin's legislative initiatives and supporting the "special military operation" they vote the same way. Such "systemic" parties are vital cogs in Russia's Kremlin-centric political machine.And if a party doesn't support the war?One such party - Yabloko - is calling for a ceasefire in Ukraine. Back in July it was the only anti-war party in Russia to be registered for the election. Twelve days later, though, the Supreme Court removed it from the ballot. That was widely interpreted as a sign of Kremlin concern that anti-war messaging could strike a chord with Russian voters.Despite Yabloko's exclusion from the party list, some of its candidates are still running in individual constituency races. Though in recent weeks growing numbers of Yabloko candidates have been detained by police, prosecuted for various offences and barred from the election."The police are carrying out a political order. That's no secret," Yabloko candidate Grigory Grishin tells me. "This way, the authorities are setting the boundaries within which they believe the elections should take place."It is well known that the demand for an end to the bloodshed in this conflict with Ukraine is very popular. In my opinion, most people in Russia now want peace and Yabloko helped people express this. That's why it's been excluded from the party lists, and why individual candidates are being barred."Image caption, Grigory Grishin says he believes demand for an end to the bloodshed in the conflict with Ukraine is very popularFor now, Grigory remains a candidate. But the police recently came to his flat."Three policemen in civilian clothes asked me to accompany them to the station, which I did. The police said I had posted what they claimed was an extremist symbol: the word 'Navalny' and that, by doing so, I had propagandised extremism via my Telegram channel."Alexei Navalny was Russia's most prominent opposition leader and Kremlin critic who died in prison in 2024. He'd been convicted on several charges, including extremism.The Russian authorities insist that the Duma elections are transparent and fair. Critics of the vote point to opposition politicians who have been forced into exile or put in prison. Last year one of the leaders of a prominent independent election monitoring group in Russia was jailed for five years. Grigory Melkonyants was convicted on charges of working with an "undesirable organisation". His election monitoring group, Golos, has shut down.Fifty miles from Moscow, in the town of Dmitrov, I see little sign of an election.In the town centre there's a memorial to "Heroes of the special military operation": local people killed fighting in Ukraine.The war is front and centre of people's minds here.Image caption, Olga's son-in-law is fighting in Russia's "special military operation""We feel it," says Olga, whose son-in-law is a soldier in the "special operation". "Because of the people who've gone to fight and the families left behind with sons, husbands, children and grandchildren there. But these elections can't influence what will happen.""I'd like us to live in a peaceful country, with no war," Polina tells me, "So that you don't have to worry that a drone will fall down in front of you."Russians have other concerns, too. Ukrainian drone attacks on Russian oil refineries have sparked widespread fuel shortages, while economic pressures are increasing."What worries me," says a barber called Ivan, "is that no matter how much you earn it's not enough. Prices are rising faster than wages. I speak to lots of people in my job. I know how hard-up they are."Expectations are low that this election will change much."Western elections and elections in Russia are completely different things," Grishin explains. "Elections in the West are a way of forming a government, which is replaced later if voters aren't satisfied."Elections in Russia never bring a change in government. At best, they're a way of influencing it, of sending a signal. But power in Russia never changed because of an election. That's how Russia is."

schema.headline: Russia's elections will have few surprises, but for the Kremlin they matter

title: Austin Tice: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds
description: US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the
body: US journalist Austin Tice, who disappeared in Syria in 2012, was kidnapped in a calculated operation which was more than a month in the planning, the BBC can reveal. A member of the group which detained Tice has also claimed the abduction was sanctioned by Syria's leader at the time, President Bashar al-Assad.Tice was seen getting into a car with a driver he knew and trusted. For years, many assumed they had stumbled upon a government checkpoint, and that the abduction of the journalist had been opportunistic. But we have uncovered evidence that, in fact, his disappearance was anything but chance.In a new BBC podcast: Where is Austin Tice? Series 3 of I'm Not A Monster Presents, we reveal the findings of a years-long investigation into what happened to Tice, who had been reporting on Syria's civil war at the time. His case has been followed closely by international media and cited by successive US presidents.Georgetown University law student Tice, who had served as a US Marines captain, was last seen in a video - blindfolded and in apparent distress - posted more than a month after his capture.As the regime fell 12 years later, tens of thousands of people emerged from the administration's prisons. Tice was not one of them. We obtained co-ordinates from an intelligence source for multiple locations US authorities suspected he could have been held at, and searched for him for more than a month, but found no sign of him.A former Syrian commander has said Tice was executed. Others have questioned this account and no remains have been found.But in the aftermath of the regime's collapse, we did uncover secret Syrian intelligence files on Tice - hundreds of pages of internal records providing the first definitive proof that it was the regime that had held the journalist.Two crucial questions remained unanswered, however: how exactly had Tice been taken in the first place? And, who was responsible for his abduction?We have spoken to a number of men from the regime involved in Tice's detention, and have reviewed recordings of discussions about it. One man we spoke to, Abu Ali, is a former member of the National Defence Forces (NDF), a militia which was fiercely loyal to Assad.He says the abduction operation began when Tice's driver - who multiple sources say had been passing the regime information for some time - told a senior NDF member that Tice was moving through rebel-held areas, reporting on the opposition.Tice had pushed into areas most journalists deemed too dangerous and was writing front-page stories for the Washington Post. The Assad regime was cracking down on anyone highlighting its human rights abuses.We have been told the NDF member Tice's driver spoke to was Sakr Rustom - not just any NDF militia contact, but nephew of Bassam al-Hassan, one of Assad's most trusted security figures and head of the NDF.The information on Tice was passed up to Hassan, Abu Ali says, who is then said to have telephoned Assad."Bring him to us," Assad replied, claims Abu Ali.Abu Ali says he was subsequently called into Hassan's office and told the president had approved the operation.But Tice was not taken immediately. The driver, Abu Ali says, suggested that he and the NDF continue watching him, to uncover more about what he was doing."He trusts me," Abu Ali recalls the driver saying.Some time later, the driver reported back that Tice's actions seemed suspicious, Abu Ali says. Tice, as a trained marine, would sometimes share his military experience with rebel fighters - according to several people we spoke to - and would correct fighters on how they used their weapons.To the men watching him, that behaviour made Tice look less like a journalist and more like someone from the CIA. The BBC has found no evidence to suggest this was the case, and a former senior US official responsible for part of Tice's case has denied he was an intelligence officer.In the days before Tice vanished, the driver made one particularly brazen move while Tice was interviewing rebel fighters. He secretly took the American's backpack, containing his MacBook, a satellite transmitter and other personal items, for regime operatives to look through, multiple sources say.On 11 August 2012, Tice celebrated his 31st birthday at a rebel safehouse on the western edge of Damascus, a few miles from Assad's presidential palace. There was a swimming pool, Free Syrian Army fighters, Taylor Swift music and whiskey, Tice revealed in what would become his final tweet."Hands down, best birthday ever," he wrote.Then came the time for Tice to leave Syria. He had told various people he was planning to take time out in Lebanon.But he was not heading to safety. He was heading to a state facility where Hassan had an office, in an area called Tahouneh on the outskirts of Damascus, according to several sources. Abu Ali was waiting there for Tice.Abu Ali says Tice's driver told him that when he drew up to the gates, he pulled out a gun.Tice laughed at first, Ali recalls the driver saying, apparently believing the man he trusted was joking. But the driver told Tice he was serious, Abu Ali says, and the journalist realised what was happening. According to Ali, Tice pulled out his chequebook and pleaded with the driver to name his price, rather than go through with the kidnap.NDF militia members then grabbed Tice, covering his eyes, Abu Ali says. Another NDF member told us he would never forget Tice's expression as he realised he had been betrayed. Abu Ali says Hassan immediately called President Assad to tell him they had the American.For years, the identity of Tice's driver has remained a mystery.The BBC spoke to more than 20 people to discover who he was, with the trail eventually leading to the city of Homs, and the family of a man called Hamid Abu Obeid.They confirmed he was the man who had driven Tice away, an account also supported by multiple NDF members. But by the time we identified him, Abu Obeid had disappeared. His family say they do not know where he is, and fear for his safety. They say they were not aware of Hamid's involvement in Tice's case, and learned about it from him afterwards.But they did give a motive for his betrayal of Tice.The Abu Obeid family, Palestinian refugees from Gaza, live in poverty. Under Syrian law they are not entitled to Syrian citizenship and live under significant restrictions. According to Hamid's brother, he had been promised a passport, Syrian citizenship, a house, and a weapon, in return for delivering Tice - life-changing rewards. But after the abduction, the family says all he got was a pistol.Then, after Assad's regime fell, Abu Obeid's wife says her husband was called by a man who knew about his involvement in Tice's case and was threatening to tell the US embassy, hoping it might help him secure asylum. Abu Obeid urged him not to. He then took some money, told his wife he was going shopping, and she says she has not seen him since. She does not know if he is in hiding, or if he has been detained or killed.Not long after he disappeared, she says masked men - some dressed in military clothes - visited and took a number of Abu Obeid's possessions, including his laptop and other devices.The wishes of Abu Obeid's wife now chillingly mirror those of Tice's mother and family. On opposite sides of a disappearance that began more than a decade ago, both families are searching for the same thing: a loved one who vanished, and an answer to where he went.

schema.headline: Austin Tice: Assad regime planned US journalist's kidnap for weeks, BBC finds

title: Chelsea: Clearlake Capital acquires full control as Todd Boehly, Mark Walter and Hansjorg Wyss sell stakes
description: Chelsea chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter have sold their stakes in the club to majority owner Clearlake Capital.It means Clearlake - led
body: Chelsea chairman Todd Boehly and director Mark Walter have sold their stakes in the club to majority owner Clearlake Capital.It means Clearlake - led by co-founders Behdad Eghbali and Jose E. Feliciano - have now acquired full control of the club.Boehly, Walter and Swiss billionaire Hansjorg Wyss each had a 12.8% stake, with Clearlake previously owning 61.5% of the Blues.In a statement, the club said Wyss "will remain an important stakeholder and partner in the ownership group".However, American Boehly will leave his role as chairman, a position he has held since 2022 when the consortium bought the club for £2.3bn from Roman Abramovich in the wake of the Russian being sanctioned by the UK government over alleged links to his country's president Vladimir Putin - something he has denied.It is understood Clearlake have paid approaching £1bn for the two stakes which amount to about a quarter of the club - although people close to the transaction maintain Chelsea's overall value is around £5bn.BBC Sport reported in August that Boehly and Walter were exploring selling their stakes.Multiple sources said talks started within Chelsea's ownership group after a rift, first apparent in 2024, led both sides to explore buying each other out.Boehly, who is a co-owner of baseball franchise the Los Angeles Dodgers, said it had been an "honour" to serve as Chelsea chairman."I would like to thank the many who helped secure a bright future for the club, including the English Premier League, the coaches and players, the talented leadership and staff at Chelsea, and the legions of dedicated fans," he added."I have valued my partnership with Clearlake and the wider ownership group, and the collective decisions and investment we have made to support the immediate and long-term success of the club. I am confident that Chelsea is well positioned for continued success under Clearlake's leadership."Boehly and Walter have also sold their shareholding in Chelsea's partner club, French Ligue 1 side Strasbourg.Since the takeover in 2022, Chelsea's highest Premier League finish is fourth in 2024-25, with the club also winning the Uefa Conference League and Fifa Club World Cup that season.The club have also had a remarkably high turnover of players over the past four years, with the initial strategy focusing on signing young players to long-term contracts.Chelsea finished 10th in the Premier League last season and appointed Xabi Alonso as their manager in the summer.Eghbali and Feliciano thanked Boehly for his "time and contribution" as chairman, saying he will "always be a part of the Chelsea story and family".They added their focus is to "continue investing in the club's infrastructure, sporting performance, player development and delivering long-term success for Chelsea and the club's supporters".Chelsea have ongoing plans either to redevelop Stamford Bridge or move to a new stadium, which sources say had created tension at times between Boehly's camp and Clearlake.A club statement said there will be "no changes to the day-to-day operations, leadership or strategy at the club" as a result of Clearlake assuming full control.Walter, the co-owner and chief executive of global finance firm Guggenheim Partners, where Boehly also began his financial career, last month sold the Los Angeles Lakers for a record $12.5bn (£9.23bn) - a year after buying a majority stake in the NBA franchise.Separately, US federal prosecutors and the Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating companies in Walter's business empire.

schema.headline: Chelsea: Clearlake Capital acquires full control as Todd Boehly, Mark Walter and Hansjorg Wyss sell stakes

title: Brynna mum's Facebook kidney plea prompts stranger to donate
description: A woman who shared a desperate plea for a kidney on Facebook has undergone a lifesaving transplant after a stranger offered to be her donor.Karen Dave
body: A woman who shared a desperate plea for a kidney on Facebook has undergone a lifesaving transplant after a stranger offered to be her donor.Karen Davey, 41, had exhausted every avenue before turning to social media, where she said she did not "want to leave her family without a mother".Gary Summerfield saw the mum-of-four's post and, after learning he was a match, donated one of his kidneys via an operation in July. "I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them," said Gary.Karen's family said they would never be able to repay Gary for his generosity, adding that it had given her "another chance to be a mum".The average wait for a deceased donor kidney transplant in the UK is two to three years, according to NHS Blood and Transplant, but if you have a living donor it can be about three to six months.This was Karen's second lifesaving transplant. She underwent a heart transplant 10 years ago, after having a heart attack aged 31 while watching her son play football.A transplant increases the risk of infection because of the medication patients need to take following the procedure, and complications led to Karen developing kidney failure. "I knew the tablets I was taking following the heart transplant would damage the kidneys so they try and keep the dose as low as possible, but we always knew when I had the heart transplant that I would probably need a kidney transplant at some point, and that is hard to deal with mentally."Karen, from Brynna, Rhondda Cynon Taf, was in stage three kidney failure when she discovered her friends and family were not matches and decided to put a plea on Facebook.She explained in her post that she has a relatively rare blood type and described the kidney failure as putting her life on hold."My main thing is the kids, I want to be around for them."Karen's eldest is now 22, and she is also grandmother to a one-year-old. "The kids were 10 years younger when I had the heart transplant, and they've been through a lot since then and the kidney was just the next hurdle," she added.Gary, a security guard from Tredegar, Blaenau Gwent, stumbled upon Karen's post by chance and felt he had to help."I saw Karen's appeal and she mentioned the children, and I thought 'Karen's a similar age to my daughter and her youngest child is the same age as my grandson', and I just thought it's terrible for the children," he said."If It was my daughter, I would be searching everywhere if we had exhausted all avenues through the family and friends, I would want a stranger to come forward. And I thought it would be selfish not to."He added: "I thought this lady needs one of my kidneys more than I need two of them."Although, Gary, 60, had never met Karen, he immediately volunteered to be tested.He underwent extensive assessments, including compatibility testing, psychological evaluations, blood tests, cholesterol checks and other medical examinations.The pair then underwent the six-hour procedure on 15 July at the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff. Gary said he never had any second thoughts.He added: "It's amazing seeing Karen today, the first time since the transplant and looking so well."For me, donating a kidney is simply up there with getting married and having my children, it's one of the top three things in my life."And she's a very deserving lady and a deserving family."Karen said she felt "100 times better" and her husband Matthew said they would always be grateful to Gary."Everyone knows what's going on in the world at the moment, it's a horrible place at times, but it really does give you hope that there is kindness in the world," he said. "We'll never, ever be able to repay Gary and the family for what they've done, and to give Karen another chance, another chance of being able to be the mother to our children and just live a life that she deserves."He has given that gift of life."Karen added: "The fact that somebody came forward and has gone through all the testing, because it's a lot of testing. For somebody to put their body through that and having a kidney taken out for somebody that they don't know, it's mind-blowing, I'm just so grateful."The couple's son Brandon, 17, said it was "amazing" to see his mum on the road to recovery after the transplant.He said: "She's looked better now than she has in a long while."It can be scary, obviously, when she's going into surgeries, but you just have to have hope. It's just amazing there's still good people out there."

schema.headline: Brynna mum's Facebook kidney plea prompts stranger to donate

title: New hope for breast cancer patients as life-extending drug now on NHS in England
description: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "Enhertu can be life-changing, and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it
body: Health Secretary Yvette Cooper said: "Enhertu can be life-changing, and this recommendation means NHS patients will finally be able to benefit from it."It is a tribute to the campaigners and charities who never stopped pressing for this."This decision will affect about 1,000 women a year with a specific type of breast cancer, HER2-low.Charity Breast Cancer Now said that while campaigners' "persistence paid off", thousands of people have missed out on access to Enhertu and many have died.The charity's chief executive, Claire Rowney, said: "Today we can finally say we did it." However, she adds that "we can't celebrate this momentous decision without remembering the devastating cost of this delay".Kate Wills, 51, understands this mix of emotions. She has HER2-low metastatic breast cancer, which has spread to her bones and lungs. But nothing about her suggests that she is terminally ill.She has a high-powered job and is a wife and mum. Her social media feed shows a full and happy life - only the occasional medical appointment hints all is not well.Kate says it has been "incredibly painful" to know that Enhertu could keep her alive for longer but she couldn't get it.The BBC understands that the drug companies Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca have not substantially lowered their prices since the drug was first rejected.The reason NICE has reversed its decision is largely because of a trade deal with the USA, where the UK government agreed to spend 25% more on medicines.As part of this, NICE has increased how much the NHS will pay for every extra year of good quality life a medication can give.This is known as a QALY (Quality-Adjusted Life Year) - and the upper threshold per QALY has gone from £30,000 to £35,000.At the end of August, NICE also introduced a different, more nuanced, way of measuring a patient's quality of life. These two changes were enough to tip the balance.It is thought that patient campaigns for Enhertu - and other drugs - have helped too.Daiichi Sankyo and AstraZeneca welcome NICE's decision, but the latter is calling for "strong collaboration" across the healthcare system to ensure "faster, more equitable patient access in the future".Breast Cancer Now's Claire Rowney says: "We are calling on the government, NICE, NHS England and the pharmaceutical industry to work together to fix this broken system, so that people with incurable metastatic breast cancer are not forced to spend precious months and years campaigning for treatments that could give them more time."Helen Knight, director of medicines evaluation at NICE, says she is pleased a "commercial solution" means the treatment can be made available on the NHS in England but adds she knows the decision "comes too late for many families"."Our role is important in ensuring NHS spending on new medicines reflects the benefits they deliver while protecting valuable health resources for other essential patient services," she says.For Kate, the thought of dying before she had to, "when there was a drug that I just could almost reach but couldn't get", was "so incredibly painful"."To know that I can get it now is absolutely everything."

schema.headline: New hope for breast cancer patients as life-extending drug now on NHS in England

title: Savannah DeMelo: USA midfielder sues doctors after on-pitch cardiac arrest
description: United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last y
body: United States women's national team player Savannah DeMelo is suing a hospital and two doctors after she suffered a cardiac arrest on the pitch last year.Midfielder DeMelo, who has seven senior caps for the USA, has filed a lawsuit against University of Louisville Health (UofL Health) for negligence.The 28-year-old, who plays for Racing Louisville, collapsed in the first half of a National Women's Soccer League (NWSL) match on 14 September 2025.According to documents, external seen by BBC Sport, the case was filed on Tuesday morning with Jefferson Circuit Court in Kentucky, where her club is based - a year and a day after her on-field collapse.DeMelo's filing claims UofL Health and two doctors, Dr Sarabjeet Suri and Dr Jennifer Daily, "failed to act as a reasonably prudent and competent medical practice, and such negligence was a substantial factor in causing DeMelo to suffer severe physical injuries, including, but not limited to, her cardiac arrest".Dr Daily, according to her online UofL biography, external, is Racing Louisville's chief medical officer. The lawsuit states DeMelo was under the care of Dr Daily from January 2024 to July 2026.It states that in March 2025, Dr Daily referred DeMelo to Dr Suri for "evaluation and treatment" after she had been complaining of chest pain, dizziness and shortness of air; Dr Suri obtained a history, performed a physical examination and ordered diagnostic tests.Nearly six months later, DeMelo suffered the cardiac arrest."She was subsequently diagnosed and treated for ventricular tachycardia [an abnormal heart rhythm]," the suit states.DeMelo, who has spent her entire professional career with Racing Louisville, has not played since her collapse.In a post to her Instagram page, external on Tuesday, De Melo - who was picked in the USA squad for the 2023 Women's World Cup and started their first two games - marked the anniversary of the incident."A year ago today, while playing soccer, I collapsed due to an undiagnosed cardiac arrhythmia, that caused me to go into cardiac arrest," she wrote."I respect and appreciate the privacy everyone has met me with while going through everything I have this year. I'll never be able to fully put into words how emotionally hard this year has been. There has been a lot of uncertainty and emotions intertwined with it all."

schema.headline: Savannah DeMelo: USA midfielder sues doctors after on-pitch cardiac arrest

title: I sent 200 DMs to companies - it was awkward but I got a job
description: Figure caption, 'I sent 200 DMs': Networking in New YorkByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Reporting fromNew YorkFor some, networking comes naturally but
body: Figure caption, 'I sent 200 DMs': Networking in New YorkByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Reporting fromNew YorkFor some, networking comes naturally but for others, the thought of approaching someone they don't know and trying to make a professional connection can fill them with dread.Whether you're looking for your first job, trying to get ahead at work or hoping to change career, building a network can help you find opportunities and make connections.Networking doesn't have to mean working a room at a formal event - it can happen in person over a coffee at work, through a chance conversation or online, through email and social media. Just under half (44%) of Gen Z say not having the right network is the biggest barrier to landing an entry-level role, according to research from LinkedIn, external.Nicole Leverich, chief communications officer at LinkedIn, shares her top tips on how to network and we took the same question to city workers in New York to find out what has worked for them. Start with the network you already have Everyone can start building their network online and "you'd be surprised how many connections you have once you connect with people you went to school with, former professors, people you met through summer jobs, family and friends," says Leverich.Don't be discouraged if your network is small as "not having a network right now doesn't mean you'll never have a network", she says.And not having obvious industry contacts shouldn't put you off.Leverich grew up in a small town in Oregon and moved to San Francisco after college without knowing anyone who worked in communications.After getting her first job, she says, "I raised my hand for a lot of the grunt work that other people didn't want to do and I built connections as I went along."Image caption, Leverich has been LinkedIn's chief communications officer for the past two yearsDo your homework - and say thank youIf you're thinking about reaching out to someone online, the key is to show you've done your homework, Leverich says.In a message you should "reference something they've posted or establish some common ground".Make sure your request is "clear and specific" and something they can do in less than five minutes. And, most importantly, don't forget to say thank you."You'd be surprised by how many people are willing to help, but I get so few thank yous," she says. "I'm not talking about anything excessive but just a 'thanks' makes you want to help next time."Build relationships before you need themNetworking can feel transactional, so to avoid that, try to build relationships before you need something from them, Leverich advises.If you know you want to work in a particular industry, "start finding people in that field a year or two before you're looking for a job".When you reach out to them, think about what you can offer them in return."If you call me and say you want a job randomly, I'm much less likely to help than if you call and ask for five minutes of advice."You also don't have to start by messaging someone directly, she says. Instead you could react to a post or drop a comment. Put in the repsIn-person networking can be more daunting, particularly early in your career, but remember that at a networking event, everyone is there to talk.To begin a conversation, start with something simple like complimenting someone's outfit, introducing yourself and asking why they're there, Leverich advises."Put in the reps and start by going to an event for just 15 minutes or half an hour and then build from there."When you want to move on, don't overthink it: "I just do the hard cut and say, 'It was great to meet you and I need to make sure I work around the room.'"If you want a softer out, something like 'I need to get a glass of water, it was great meeting you' can work."'Don't be afraid of hearing no'Image caption, Taylor and Vicky both say networking helped them get the job they are in nowOf course, knowing what you're supposed to do is one thing but actually walking up to a stranger and starting a conversation, or even messaging someone out of the blue online, is another.Taylor Crow who works in sales says she's "fairly good" at networking as it was something she prioritised at university. "I sent over 200 cold DMs on LinkedIn and reached out to people in the companies I wanted to work at while I was studying." She admits it was "so awkward" but it was something she had to do to land the job she wanted. Her colleague Vicky Peterlin, 24, agrees. "It's not about being good at networking but more about not being afraid to reach out to people. "I had thoughts about how I'm not qualified to have these conversations but then you realise there are no rules and sending out emails and messages are free and easy."The worst that can happen is that they say no and that's ok." Katherine Leopold, a tutor at Greenwich Business School, echoes this. She says the biggest hurdle is making the first move but if you don't take the step you are "ruling yourself out". The number of applications that organisations are dealing with is "absolutely enormous" so try to meet employers in person and show them your total authentic story, she advises."Ensure you say to them, 'I have this skill, I have this piece of knowledge, so I'm confident that your team is stronger with me in it.'"'Say what your goal is'Madison Brown works in tech partnerships, having previously worked in corporate jobs for 10 years.Image caption, Madison says it's important to be authentic and intentional when reaching out to peopleHe gets a lot of young people reaching out to him for career advice and opportunities, and says many of them could be much clearer in what they are looking for."There's nothing wrong with saying what your goal is or what you want to get out of this interaction." He adds that it's important to be yourself and "more doors will open if you are authentic".

title: King's 'astonishing outburst' and 'heartbreak' after search for missing Noah
description: The new allegations made in Earl Spencer's book are on several front pages. The Daily Mirror , externaldescribes as "shocking" his claim that within d
body: The new allegations made in Earl Spencer's book are on several front pages. The Daily Mirror , externaldescribes as "shocking" his claim that within days of Princess Diana's death the-then Prince Charles told him that she would be forgotten soon enough.According to the Daily Telegraph, external a source close to the King says the alleged comment was "just not in his nature" especially not at that time when he was "absolutely grief-stricken".The Palace's rejection of the claims is also on the Sun's , externalfront page, under the headline "Recollections may vary..... again."The Times, external says the row between Earl Spencer and the King will be seen as a further crisis for the monarchy. The paper says the Royal Family is preparing for a series of allegations in the book.People close to the artificial intelligence companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, have told the Financial Times, external that proposals - put forward in recent days by their bosses, on how to constrain AI's development - are creating tensions among staff.The paper says one of the ideas is to embed outside evaluators within the labs to oversee model development, but some fear this could compromise the security of their prized technology.Writing in the Daily Express, external, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, argues that Andy Burnham will drag Britain back into the 1970s. She says the government wants to spend more and tax more.The i Paper, external highlights the prime minister's pledge that the government will exercise the "highest degree of prudence" in next month's Budget. The paper also says the Chancellor John Healey is likely to increase capital gains tax.The Guardian, external reports that plans have been drawn up to "double up" prisoners in temporary prefabricated cells built for one person, because of a shortage of prison spaces in England and Wales. The paper says using the prefabricated cells to house two inmates could increase the capacity of the prison estate by 476. The Ministry of Justice says it is "pulling every lever available" to ensure there is space to lock up dangerous offenders.And finally the Daily Mail, external says it's spoken to outraged parents in Somerset after a new headteacher of Frome Community College suspended 25 pupils in the first week of term. The headteacher Dan Jeffries says the punishments were for "persistent disruption," but some parents likened his strict regime to that on a military base.

schema.headline: King's 'astonishing outburst' and 'heartbreak' after search for missing Noah

title: Interest rates hold expected but Bank of England facing tough choices
description: The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%.However, o
body: The Bank uses interest rates to control inflation, which charts the rising cost of living. It aims to keep inflation at a target rate of 2%.However, official figures released on Wednesday showed the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) measure of inflation had risen to 3.1% in August from 2.9% in July, pushing it to its highest rate in six months.The acceleration was driven by rises in the cost of petrol, diesel and airfares. Economists expect that higher global energy costs will feed through to food and fuel prices paid by consumers, meaning the inflation rate is yet to peak.The MPC will be aware that, citing the Middle East conflict and warning inflation was "set to remain well above" its 2% target for some time, the European Central Bank recently raised interest rates to 2.5%.In addition, the US Federal Reserve raised its interest rate to 3.75%-4% for similar reasons on Wednesday.However, MPC members will also be keen not to put pressure on employers and further lower the prospects for those seeking a job.Dame DeAnne Julius, a former member of the MPC, told the BBC that there was a "reasonable chance" of a rate hike.But she told the Today programme she did not believe the UK's economy was deteriorating, pointing to a steady unemployment rate and economic growth being "quite a bit better than it has been"."Our economy is in transition... I think it is actually improving," she said.Households feel the impact of a rising Bank rate through higher borrowing costs, but can benefit from more generous savings rates.Given the global picture, and market expectations of a higher Bank rate, a host of major lenders have already increased the cost of new fixed-rate mortgages in recent days.Andrew Montlake, chief executive of mortgage broker Coreco, said that the latest data showed that "the inflation dragon has not been fully slain"."If inflation proves sticky, lenders' funding costs stay under pressure, which makes cheaper mortgages harder to deliver," he said."We are already seeing lenders reprice upwards, so this will do little to calm things down. Borrowers should not panic, but anyone approaching the end of a fixed rate should start looking early, secure an option and keep reviewing it."The average two-year fixed residential mortgage rate is at its highest since 11 May, at 5.77%, while the average five-year is at its highest since 8 November 2023, at 5.83%, according to financial information service Moneyfacts.Savers may be offered more generous returns, but the spending power of their savings could be eroded by the rising cost of living."It's almost impossible to time things just right, so I would urge households to focus on what's best for them now, in the medium term and in the longer term," said Harriet Guevara, chief savings officer at Nottingham Building Society."For savers, regularly check that your savings are earning a competitive return and that you have the right balance between easy access and money you can afford to put away for longer."

title: Man Utd 2-3 Brighton: Michael Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure after loss
description: Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead.That is the context to the shocki
body: Sir Alex Ferguson was St Mirren manager the last time Manchester United lost at Old Trafford having taken a 2-0 lead.That is the context to the shocking Carabao Cup third-round exit his old club suffered against Brighton on Wednesday.It is a period of time that encompasses the legendary Scot's dynasties at Aberdeen as well as United. The Class of '92 were in nappies when John Pratt scored the winner for Tottenham on 4 September 1976.After holding protests inside and outside the ground before Sunday's loss to 10-man Manchester City, United supporters made their feelings known about their latest embarrassment in three ways.Most fans simply left as the players embarked on their post-match lap of appreciation.Some of those who remained booed, as they had done when their side fell behind 21 minutes from time.By the time they approached the tunnel, close to United's 'singing section', supporters were asking head coach Michael Carrick and his players 'what was that?'. Their wording was somewhat more colourful.It is not certain where 15-year-old JJ Gabriel was while all this was taking place, but nothing happened that would make him think he had got it wrong by turning his back on the club.Indeed, it is quite possible, probable indeed, that the promised senior debut would have been scrapped given the game situation - and the fact skipper Bruno Fernandes was among the experienced players introduced in the frantic final stages."Of course we can turn it around, we have got some really good players," said Carrick. "It feels bad because we haven't had a great week or two, or three weeks."Carrick's side have won twice this season, against newly promoted Ipswich at home after falling behind, and Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in the Champions League. They have now lost on three occasions, more defeats than Carrick experienced in 17 matches after replacing Ruben Amorim in January.Carrick has been around Manchester United long enough to know the pressure losing runs can build."I don't feel under pressure," he said. "Either way, that doesn't bother me one bit."I understand what goes on outside and how the world works, but it doesn't bother me. What bothers me is winning games, having a good feeling around the place and a good feeling around the group to know we're moving in a good direction."The problem is it doesn't feel as though they are moving in a good direction. There were certainly not many positives to take from this mess.The obvious one was Shea Lacey, who marked his first senior start with a well-taken eighth-minute goal. It meant he became the first teenager to score on his first United start since Marcus Rashford in February 2016.Lacey was one of eight changes made by Carrick. Defensively, those changes were not a success.Diogo Dalot was one of the three players to keep their place. His form has deserted him. Noussair Mazraoui is the back-up left-back, which only heightens the debate over the wisdom not to buy one before the transfer window closed. Leny Yoro and Ayden Heaven looked like the inexperienced defenders they are. In midfield Manchester United were overrun.Yet again, Rashford threatened without managing a goal or an assist. He came closest to levelling when he sped beyond the Brighton defence, but his shot was saved by Jason Steele."The longer the game went, the more we had control," was the concise assessment of Brighton boss Fabian Hurzeler. "I thought we deserved to win."Carrick didn't dispute the assessment.Carrick's greatest sadness was for Lacey, who should have had his name in lights but instead was part of a team scuttling off the pitch to the sound of boos and harsher criticism."It's a shame that Shea's moment, such a great moment for him, for his family, his friends and the whole academy... to have an academy player come in and have a moment like that gets a bit lost unfortunately," said Carrick."It won't for him when things settle down but, as we sit here now, it feels that it was a long time ago."Carrick also addressed the Gabriel situation."He's a young boy, he's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players, their welfare, their wellbeing, their exposure... we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation," he explained.But ultimately, for any manager, the assessment of their work comes through results."Being here toughens you up over a period of time," Carrick said. "It depends how you deal with it. You've got to deal with it in a way where you can cope with it and you can bring out the best in yourself. However you do that, with your motivation and the confidence deep within yourself to know we can win football matches."We've gone out of the cup tonight, and the feeling around the place feels bigger than that. I'm honest enough to say that's how it feels. But it doesn't have to be like that. If we win football matches again, it can go in a different direction."Manchester United have one more game before the international break, at Fulham on Sunday.For the general wellbeing of the club, Carrick's team really need to win.Speaking on Sky Sports, former England midfielder Jamie Redknapp said he wasn't sure they will."Right now, they're miles off it," he said. "It doesn't matter how good the manager is, if you don't have the right players it makes it really difficult."There's a reason why the other managers have struggled. Sooner or later the pressure's always going to come on."This weekend becomes a huge game. He doesn't need another poor result, otherwise all of a sudden you're going into the international break and everyone's talking about you. The winners tonight are the players who didn't play."

schema.headline: Man Utd 2-3 Brighton: Michael Carrick 'not bothered' by pressure after loss

title: JJ Gabriel: Man Utd's 15-year-old interests Real Madrid
description: Real Madrid are among the clubs trying to sign Manchester United academy player JJ Gabriel.Earlier this week, the 15-year-old sent United formal notic
body: Real Madrid are among the clubs trying to sign Manchester United academy player JJ Gabriel.Earlier this week, the 15-year-old sent United formal notice he wants to cancel his registration with immediate effect, but the club can challenge the request.It is understood a number of major teams across Europe, including Barcelona, Paris St-Germain and Bayern Munich, have a firm interest in the forward, but multiple sources have described Real's efforts to sign him as strong.The Spanish side want to recruit the teenager immediately and position him in Real Madrid Castilla - the club's recognised reserve team.Unlike in England, Castilla play in senior football and are in the regionalised third league of the Spanish system. Last season, they were coached by Alvaro Arbeloa, who then took over the senior Real side following Xabi Alonso's dismissal and has since moved to Fulham.Thiago Pitarch, who was 18 at the start of last season, played for Castilla in a Premier League International Cup encounter against Southampton in October, and made 16 senior appearances across the campaign.Sources close to Gabriel, who turns 16 on 6 October, feel let down by United, arguing promises around the pathway to the first team have not been kept. The club say it was anticipated Gabriel would become their youngest senior player by playing in Wednesday night's EFL Cup tie with Brighton. Given they lost 3-2 after leading 2-0, it is debatable whether that would have actually happened.United have not given up hope of keeping Gabriel, though they are unsure precisely why he wants to leave.It is understood the player is not currently training with the club.Speaking after the Brighton game, head coach Michael Carrick, who gave the youngster his senior debut during the pre-season match with Atletico Madrid in Stockholm said everyone needed to be mindful of Gabriel's age."I just think we've got to be really careful of the whole situation," he said."He's a young boy. He's 15, and for me, definitely, and from a club point of view, looking after our younger players - their welfare, their well-being, their exposure - we've got to be really conscious of that in this situation."Sources close to Gabriel have dismissed concerns over the player's age and physicality and feel the likes of Max Dowman, who made his debut for Arsenal at the age of 15 last season, show a willingness to trust youth in a way they do not see at United.Chelsea are also believed to have a major interest in the teenager.Any imminent move away from Old Trafford for Gabriel is complicated because of rules regarding the registration of young players.United say Gabriel's registration runs to the end of the season. It would be easier for him to leave United then, when he will be 16.However, as Gabriel has an EU passport, it is possible he will be allowed to join a club within European Union borders on his 16th birthday.

schema.headline: JJ Gabriel: Man Utd's 15-year-old interests Real Madrid

title: Hertfordshire boy, 13, is new voice of Thomas the Tank Engine
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Harry Sparkes said he kept his role a secret from his school friendsByDanny FullbrookA 13-year-old schoolboy has
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Harry Sparkes said he kept his role a secret from his school friendsByDanny FullbrookA 13-year-old schoolboy has made his voice-acting debut as Thomas the Tank Engine in a new animated series.Harry Sparkes, from Harpenden, Hertfordshire, stars in Thomas & Friends: Railway Stories alongside Crazy Rich Asians actor Henry Golding, who narrates the series in a role made famous by Sir Ringo Starr.For nine months, Sparkes kept his weekly recording sessions secret from his classmates by telling them he was attending physiotherapy for a foot injury."It feels amazing, because I played and watched Thomas as a kid, and now I get to be Thomas. It just feels insane," he said.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The new series sees Thomas and his friends return to 3D animationSparkes added that he thought his friends would be shocked to find out he was voicing the character.He said he was excited he got "to be part of something which kids from the next generation will get to grow up to watch".Franchise owners Mattel teased the new series will "introduce fans to a refreshed world of Sodor, while still celebrating the iconic railway action we have all known and loved since its debut as a classic book in 1945".Image source, ReutersImage caption, Henry Golding, who starred in 2019 films Last Christmas and The Gentleman, narrates the seriesThe character first appeared in The Railway Series, by children's author Reverend Wilbert Awdry.Golding said he was in the "shadow of giants" following in the footsteps of Sir Ringo and Pierce Brosnan, who narrated a 2008 movie special called Thomas & Friends: The Great Discovery. Golding added: "I think we bring a new spin and a new sort of excitement to Thomas, and we're kind of bringing it back up to date, which is the exciting part."Thomas & Friends Railway Stories launches on YouTube later with a special episode before airing on Milkshake! in October. A full series will debut in early 2027.Do you have a story suggestion for Beds, Herts or Bucks? Contact us below.Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: Hertfordshire boy, 13, is new voice of Thomas the Tank Engine

title: Max vs 100: Verstappen overtakes 100 amateur karters in just 14 laps
description: Max Verstappen needed just 14 laps and 35 minutes to overtake 100 amateur drivers in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone.The four-time Formula 1
body: Max Verstappen needed just 14 laps and 35 minutes to overtake 100 amateur drivers in an exhibition go-kart race at Silverstone.The four-time Formula 1 world champion had a maximum of 35 laps and 75 minutes to pass everyone on an adapted track at the grand prix circuit in Northamptonshire.Red Bull's Verstappen, 28, was up to 37th by the end of a chaotic first lap in which many drivers crashed or spun out, resulting in racing being briefly suspended."When I went to the grid and I saw where I had to start, with 100 karts in front of me, I was a little bit worried," he said."After my first lap with all the carnage, I did think 'OK, we have got this under control'. From there on, I could really have a lot of fun trying to hunt them all down."Once I started getting into a rhythm and was able to overtake them one by one and saw the gap closing, that was really exciting."The ruthless Dutchman, who warned participants "it's not a charity event" on race radio, moved into 10th by the start of lap six and was in fourth by lap 10, with each driver he passed having to retire.At that stage, the field - made up of TV, sport and social media personalities, with no professional racing drivers - consisted of just Dutch F1 journalist Jacky Martens, Red Bull engine builder Lewis Osler and YouTuber Zac Alsop.All three were given an extra 'fast lap' where they could cut a corner of the track to try to hold off Verstappen for longer, but he inevitably reeled them in.Martens, who was on pole position after qualifying, was the final driver to be passed as Verstappen completed his challenge with 40 minutes and 21 laps to spare.Verstappen began his racing career as a junior in karting and won four consecutive F1 titles between 2021 and 2024."It was great to just be back in a go-kart again and go back to basics, it reminded me of racing back in the day," he added."It's a really beautiful track and well designed. I had a great day and it was good to come out with the win."

schema.headline: Max vs 100: Verstappen overtakes 100 amateur karters in just 14 laps
